title: Non-target feeding on cultivated artichoke by Cassida rubiginosa (Coleoptera: Chrysomelidae) reflects behavioral flexibility rather than host-range expansion
content:
Abstract
Spillover by weed biological control agents onto non-target plants can raise concern that feeding represents the early stages of a host shift. However, non-target feeding may instead reflect behavioral flexibility caused by related non-target plants nearby or declining primary-host quality. To distinguish between these outcomes, we investigated host-use behavior and body mass as a fitness proxy in the thistle tortoise beetle, Cassida rubiginosa Müller, on artichoke, Cynara scolymus L. Cassida rubiginosa is a biological control agent of Cirsium arvense (L.) Scop. in New Zealand, where adult feeding on artichoke has been reported. Adults collected from artichoke and thistle were offered both plants in paired-choice assays. We measured feeding initiation, the first plant fed upon, feeding-hole number, resting position, initial body mass, and mass change over 24 h. Artichoke-origin beetles initiated feeding more rapidly and were more likely than thistle-origin beetles to begin feeding on artichoke. They showed no strong initial preference between plants, whereas thistle-origin beetles overwhelmingly initiated feeding on thistle. Thistle received more feeding holes, and beetles from both origins rested predominantly on thistle after 24 h. Artichoke-origin beetles were initially lighter but gained more mass with increasing feeding activity when both plants were available. Although artichoke-origin beetles initially accepted artichoke more readily, their subsequent feeding and resting occurred primarily on thistle. This overall preference for thistle, together with the lower initial mass of artichoke-origin beetles, is consistent with behavioral plasticity leading to opportunistic spillover onto a cultivated, suboptimal relative of the target weed rather than a host shift.
